title: People's Choice

jokes.text: Larry fishing to find out if his name came up for the People's Choice hosting gig while pretending not to care
jokes.setup: Artie mentions he's producing the People's Choice Awards. Larry says 'Fine. Congratulations.' and the conversation drifts to Oahu — then Larry suddenly pivots back.
jokes.punchline: 'Did my name even come up for the people's-choice thing? It just seems like that's the kind of thing they'd ask me to do, that's all.'
jokes.explanation: Classic Larry Sanders character comedy: he can't simply ask what he wants, so he performs indifference and then betrays it immediately. The long detour through Oahu makes the eventual pivot land harder. High character integration because this is the defining Larry trait — insecure, status-obsessed, incapable of directness.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I pay a cabana boy to wheel me down to the beach every day on a stretcher like a coma patient.

jokes.text: Artie on his Oahu vacation: 'I pay a cabana boy to wheel me down to the beach every day on a stretcher like a coma patient.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks what Artie does in Oahu, implying vacations are leisure and fun.
jokes.punchline: Artie describes a deliberately decrepit, helpless vacation image with total deadpan confidence.
jokes.explanation: A nearly perfect Artie line. The image of being wheeled on a stretcher 'like a coma patient' is specific, eccentric, and entirely in character for Rip Torn's grizzled, world-weary producer. The follow-up 'Is that included in the package?' from Larry is the ideal straight-man topper. Highly quotable, original image, zero fat in the delivery. Justifies the 8+ score.

dialogue.line: Is that included in the package?

jokes.text: Larry asks 'Is that included in the package?' after Artie describes being wheeled to the beach on a stretcher like a coma patient.
jokes.setup: Artie's bizarre vacation description invites sympathy or confusion.
jokes.punchline: Larry responds as if this is a normal vacation amenity to be evaluated.
jokes.explanation: A well-timed straight-man topper that extends Artie's joke. Doesn't try to top the image, just plays into it with perfect economy. Good structure; earns its place as part of a two-beat joke.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: It just seems like that's the kind of thing they'd ask me to do, that's all.

jokes.text: Hank insisting on doing 'one more take, just for fun' of a commercial parody; the director mutters 'There is a finite amount of videotape in the world.'
jokes.setup: Hank, deeply proud of his improv, wants another take after being told they have it.
jokes.punchline: The director's deadpan existential exasperation: 'There is a finite amount of videotape in the world.'
jokes.explanation: Highly economical and dry. The line is a perfect expression of behind-the-scenes frustration with a difficult performer, scaled to cosmic absurdity. Works on its own and deepens the Hank characterization.

dialogue.line: There is a finite amount of videotape in the world.

jokes.text: Hank's forbidden coconut take plays — 'Mmm, tastes a little like coconut.' — after the director said it was the last take.
jokes.setup: The director emphatically declares the next take is the last. Hank has been told not to do the coconut line.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Hank doing the coconut line anyway.
jokes.explanation: The show cuts directly to the thing it just said wouldn't happen. Economy is near-perfect — no additional dialogue, just the visual/audio evidence of Hank's incorrigibility. Sets up the coconut running gag that pays dividends for the whole episode.

dialogue.line: Some shave creams are coconut-scented, so it's not funny.

jokes.text: Larry's argument against the coconut line: 'Some shave creams are coconut-scented, so it's not funny.'
jokes.setup: Larry is furious the coconut line aired and needs to justify why it's wrong.
jokes.punchline: His definitive comedic logic — a product existing in coconut scent disqualifies the joke — is both plausibly correct and hilariously specific as the hill he dies on.
jokes.explanation: Larry's rationale is both valid comedy theory and a pitch-perfect portrait of a control-freak host who has to be right. The specificity ('coconut-scented') elevates this above a simple 'that's not funny' complaint. Good character integration — this is exactly how Larry would argue.

dialogue.line: Should I go talk to him?
I wouldn't talk to him at all.
Then you go talk to him.

jokes.text: 'And we have 22 takes with him saying chicken, one of which we'll use.'
jokes.setup: The chaos of managing Hank's ego through the shoot.
jokes.punchline: 22 takes — a quietly staggering number delivered with perfect flatness.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully understated beat. The number 22 does all the work — it conveys the absurdity of working with Hank without any editorializing. Economy is the chief virtue here.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: How could she not be available?

jokes.text: The whole office debating who should go talk to Hank about the coconut line, ending in a circular non-resolution.
jokes.setup: Someone has to go soothe Hank's feelings. No one wants to do it.
jokes.punchline: After multiple assignments and reassignments — 'I wouldn't talk to him at all' / 'Then you go talk to him' / 'Should I go?' / 'I wouldn't' — nothing is resolved, just deferred.
jokes.explanation: Good ensemble cringe comedy — the bureaucratic cowardice of a writers' room trying to avoid an uncomfortable conversation is perfectly observed. The circular structure (everyone agrees someone should go, no one goes) is the point. Slightly long but the absurd loop earns it.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I gave her her first orgasm.

jokes.text: Artie on Sally Kirkland: 'I gave her her first orgasm.' / 'Oh, well, then she's perfect.'
jokes.setup: Artie is pushing for Sally Kirkland as a guest for the People's Choice, and Larry expresses skepticism.
jokes.punchline: Artie's credential for vouching for her is that he gave her her first orgasm; Larry immediately treats this as a valid booking criterion.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is a normal casting conversation; the punchline is Artie's absurd — but delivered as entirely professional — credential. What makes it exceptional is Larry's response: not shock, not disgust, just 'Oh, well, then she's perfect.' The transaction is complete. Both lines are needed; neither works alone. Pure character comedy — only Artie could say this, and only Larry would accept it. Earns the 8.5+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Oh, well, then she's perfect.

jokes.text: 'Send her roses, long-stem and a limo. She'll do it.'
jokes.setup: After establishing his personal 'credential' with Sally Kirkland.
jokes.punchline: Artie's follow-through: his insider knowledge of exactly how to get her — roses and a limo — presented as standard show-business wisdom born from intimate history.
jokes.explanation: The topper on the Sally Kirkland bit. Artie's practical knowledge of how to procure Sally Kirkland — presented as pure logistics — deepens the absurdity of the previous line while staying in character. The specificity ('long-stem') is doing extra work.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Maybe he'll do pump it up. That's my favorite song.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown
dialogue.line: I think he'd rather do something off the new album.

jokes.text: Larry wants Elvis Costello to play 'Pump It Up' — his favorite — but the booker warns he's temperamental and would 'rather do something off the new album.'
jokes.setup: Larry expresses genuine fan enthusiasm for Elvis Costello.
jokes.punchline: The friction between fan Larry (who wants his favorite) and professional Larry (who has to manage a temperamental guest) is established — foreshadowing the episode's later Elvis disaster.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup comedy. The joke is modest — Larry's fan desire vs. reality — but earns points in retrospect as plant/payoff for the Elvis meltdown. Not especially quotable on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: So I thought I'd heard that song somewhere before. I had to bring it up.

jokes.text: The Michael Bolton incident: 'Remember what happened last time you talked to Michael Bolton? So I thought I'd heard that song somewhere before. I had to bring it up.'
jokes.setup: Larry suggests he could personally ask Elvis Costello to play 'Pump It Up.'
jokes.punchline: He's banned from talking to guests after apparently accusing Michael Bolton of plagiarism mid-interaction.
jokes.explanation: This is a gem of an offhand reference. The Michael Bolton plagiarism accusation (Bolton was genuinely embroiled in copyright controversy at the time) is weaponized as backstory to reveal Larry's inability to filter himself with guests. 'So I thought I'd heard that song somewhere before. I had to bring it up.' — the self-aware resignation makes it. High character integration; only Larry would do this AND feel slightly justified.

dialogue.line: Keep it down because he could be lurking out there.
He does that?

jokes.text: Chicken take plays correctly, then Hank's coconut take is shown 'just so we say we saw it.'
jokes.setup: Phil presents the commercial parody edit.
jokes.punchline: Screening Hank's rejected coconut take as a curiosity/joke — 'just so we say we saw it' — after all the drama about it.
jokes.explanation: A solid callback beat that keeps the coconut running gag alive. Phil's understated 'just so we say we saw it' is funny because it treats Hank's work like a medical anomaly to be documented. Competent running gag maintenance.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Al 'harelip' hartman?

jokes.text: Hank auditioning as announcer for the People's Choice by doing the announcer's line, then complaining: 'Al 'Harelip' Hartman? No, no. This guy, he has no verve, no personality.'
jokes.setup: Artie tells Hank the People's Choice already has an announcer.
jokes.punchline: Hank spontaneously does the announcer line, then immediately critiques the real announcer's work — transparently lobbying for his own job.
jokes.explanation: Classic Hank: can't ask for what he wants directly, so demonstrates it while complaining about the competition. The name 'Al Harelip Hartman' is a bonus absurdist detail. Strong character integration — this is quintessential Hank behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: And he drinks.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: So do I. That's why I like him.

jokes.text: 'And he drinks.' / 'So do I. That's why I like him.'
jokes.setup: Hank complains the existing announcer is a 'robot' with no personality.
jokes.punchline: Artie's defense: the guy drinks. Hank's counter: he also drinks, which is why he likes him — but that still doesn't mean he should have the job.
jokes.explanation: A perfectly constructed two-line exchange. Artie's non sequitur defense ('he drinks') is funny; Hank's self-incriminating 'So do I. That's why I like him' is funnier. Maximum economy — the whole joke is two lines, and both are good. The logic is absurd but feels completely natural for these characters.

dialogue.line: How many things can he have up his ass at once?

jokes.text: 'He has a hair up his ass because I won't hire him as the announcer for the people's choice.' / 'He's got that coconut line up his ass.' / 'How many things can he have up his ass at once?'
jokes.setup: Trying to diagnose why Hank is upset and won't film the commercial parody segment.
jokes.punchline: The anatomical metaphor for grievances escalates — coconut line AND announcer job — until someone asks the logical limit question.
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in escalation via a repeated anatomical idiom. The setup ('hair up his ass') is conventional; adding the coconut line creates the callback; 'How many things can he have up his ass at once?' is the logical conclusion that brings the house down. The escalation structure is tight and the payoff question is perfectly framed.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You folks came on a very rare night where you get to see me fuck up 3 jokes in a row. Don't take it for granted.

jokes.text: Larry's on-air mea culpa to the audience: 'You folks came on a very rare night where you get to see me fuck up 3 jokes in a row. Don't take it for granted.'
jokes.setup: Larry has visibly botched several jokes during the taping.
jokes.punchline: He addresses it directly and ironically, framing his failure as a privilege for the audience.
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta moment. Larry's ability to spin public failure into a backhanded gift to the audience ('Don't take it for granted') is simultaneously charming, self-deprecating, and egotistical — all Larry in one sentence. 'I won't fuck up the rest of the night' as the kicker is perfect. The joke is funny within the show AND as a commentary on how late-night hosts handle bombs. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What a shit crowd. What a shit, shit crowd.

jokes.text: 'What are they doing, bringing these busloads in from the English-as-a-second-language program?'
jokes.setup: Larry continues ranting about the audience quality backstage.
jokes.punchline: His theory for why they didn't laugh: they literally can't understand English — an absurd, self-serving rationalization.
jokes.explanation: Larry's self-exculpating logic taken to a specific, absurd extreme. Rather than accepting his jokes bombed, he invents an audience deficiency. The specificity of 'English-as-a-second-language program' is the key — it's exactly the kind of paranoid, almost plausible excuse Larry would reach for.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: What are they doing, bringing these busloads in from the english-as-a-second-language program?

jokes.text: 'I'm only smiling because the audience is looking at me, and I'm a professional.'
jokes.setup: Larry is still ranting about the audience while they're still visible/nearby.
jokes.punchline: He acknowledges, mid-rant, that his current smile is entirely performative — a confession of professional inauthenticity delivered with total deadpan.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's single best line. It encapsulates the entire show's thesis — the gap between performed warmth and genuine contempt — in one compact, devastating sentence. 'I'm a professional' as the punchline is extraordinary: it's both a legitimate credential and an admission of complete fakery. Maximum character integration (this line could ONLY be Larry Sanders), maximum economy, and it crystallizes a truth about celebrity performance that resonates beyond the show. Justifies 8.6.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I'm only smiling because the audience is looking at me, and I'm a professional.

jokes.text: After all the 'shit crowd' venting, someone tells Larry it's a great crowd tonight — he agrees instantly: 'Yeah, I know, shit crowd.' then pivots to logistics.
jokes.setup: Staff member offers a positive spin on the crowd.
jokes.punchline: Larry agrees by restating his own negative assessment — 'Yeah, I know, shit crowd' — completely unaware of or indifferent to the contradiction.
jokes.explanation: A quick, perfectly timed callback beat. The comedy is in Larry's brain being so locked onto 'shit crowd' that he processes agreement as agreement — even when the message is opposite. Economy is excellent; it's a blink-and-miss-it beat that rewards attention.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Thank God. I thought it was something that might have to do with the show we're taping now.

jokes.text: Paul Reiser dropping out of the People's Choice — Artie's relief that it's not about the show being taped right now.
jokes.setup: News arrives mid-taping that Paul Reiser dropped out of the People's Choice Awards.
jokes.punchline: 'Thank God. I thought it was something that might have to do with the show we're taping now.' — Artie's priorities are the show in front of him; celebrity guests quitting other shows is a relief.
jokes.explanation: A solid character beat for Artie — he's the consummate professional who only cares about the work immediately in front of him. The comic reversal (news that sounds bad is actually a relief) is well-executed if not spectacular.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Andalé, felipe. Vamanos.

jokes.text: 'Aw, the thrill of live-to-tape television. Andalé, Felipe. Vámonos.'
jokes.setup: The editor panics that the commercial parody airs in 20 minutes and can't be recut.
jokes.punchline: Artie responds with a Spanish dismissal and fake enthusiasm for the logistical crisis.
jokes.explanation: Artie's Hemingway-esque crisis management delivered as casual sarcasm. The Spanish is an inspired touch — it signals urgency while undercutting it simultaneously. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: You'll only have to strip at the end of the show.

jokes.text: Artie guilts Larry into hosting the People's Choice as 'a favor,' and Larry negotiates out of dance numbers — then accepts when he's told he only has to strip at the end.
jokes.setup: Artie asks Larry to host as a personal favor. Larry resists with a list of legitimate objections.
jokes.punchline: 'You'll only have to strip at the end of the show. How about it?' Larry: 'That's the favor to you, isn't it?' — he caves, having accomplished nothing in negotiations.
jokes.explanation: The strip joke is a good subversion — it swaps a real demand for an absurd one and Larry still accepts. 'That's the favor to you, isn't it?' is a nice self-aware admission that he's been played. Solid character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: News travels fast, doesn't it?

jokes.text: The commercial parody airs with Hank's coconut line — after all the effort to remove it.
jokes.setup: The whole episode has been about keeping the coconut line out of the broadcast.
jokes.punchline: It airs anyway. 'Larry Sanders' Toiletries for the Hungry Man. Thank you.' then Hank: 'Mmm, tastes a little like coconut.'
jokes.explanation: The satisfying collapse of all the episode's coconut-line scheming into one broadcast fait accompli. The structure is excellent — the payoff is proportional to all the buildup. The absurd commercial title ('Toiletries for the Hungry Man') is a bonus visual gag. Economy is perfect: it just plays, no comment needed.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: You're cohosting with fucking superman.

jokes.text: Stevie (Larry's agent) on a car phone: 'Larry, this is a partnership. You don't say yes. We say yes.'
jokes.setup: Larry has agreed to host the People's Choice as a favor to Artie without telling his agent.
jokes.punchline: Stevie's correction reveals the agent-client power dynamic: Larry's autonomy is actually a joint venture the agent controls.
jokes.explanation: Sharp industry satire compressed into one sentence. The 'we say yes' framing is a perfect distillation of how agents think. Good economy; quotable in a showbiz context.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Cohosting detracts from your essential specialness in the marketplace.

jokes.text: Larry discovers he's cohosting with Rita Moreno and Dean Cain: 'You're cohosting with fucking Superman.'
jokes.setup: Larry agreed to 'host' the People's Choice as a favor; Stevie reveals it's actually a cohosting gig.
jokes.punchline: 'You're cohosting with Rita Moreno and Dean Cain.' / 'Who's Dean Cain?' / 'Superman.' / 'You're cohosting with fucking Superman.'
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured three-step escalation: 'Dean Cain' means nothing → 'Superman' recontextualizes → 'You're cohosting with fucking Superman' is the explosion. The fact that Stevie delivers this as if it's the worst imaginable indignity is perfect. The joke also works as celebrity status satire — Dean Cain as Superman representing the tier below Larry. Earns the 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Stevie
dialogue.line: Who are you, kathie Lee all of a sudden?

jokes.text: Stevie: 'Arthur's fucking you, Larry.' / 'Cohosting detracts from your essential specialness in the marketplace.'
jokes.setup: Larry defends taking the cohosting gig as doing Artie a favor.
jokes.punchline: Stevie's agent-speak: 'Cohosting detracts from your essential specialness in the marketplace' — then making Larry repeat it back like a mantra.
jokes.explanation: The phrase 'essential specialness in the marketplace' is wonderful industry-speak satire, funny because it's the kind of thing agents actually say. Making Larry repeat it like a child in therapy is a great comedic escalation. The whole Stevie scene is a tight, well-observed satire of the talent-agent relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Darlene
dialogue.line: At the daily planet newspaper in metropolis.

jokes.text: 'Who are you, Kathie Lee all of a sudden?'
jokes.setup: Stevie lectures Larry about protecting his brand and marketplace position.
jokes.punchline: Larry dismisses the earnest career advice by comparing Stevie to Kathie Lee Gifford — a contemporary celebrity known for relentless self-promotion and saccharine sincerity.
jokes.explanation: A topical celebrity name-drop that earns its place because the Kathie Lee Gifford comparison is specific and apt — she was the queen of brand-protecting earnestness in this era. Not timeless, but works in context. Economy is good.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: It's another pleat in your cape.

jokes.text: Stevie makes Larry repeat: 'Cohosting detracts from my essential specialness in the marketplace.'
jokes.setup: Stevie is trying to drill his branding point into Larry's head.
jokes.punchline: Having a late-night talk show host repeat agent mantras like a child in school is inherently demeaning and funny — especially because Larry complies.
jokes.explanation: Functional extension of the agent parody. The compliance is the joke — Larry is fully under Stevie's thumb despite his on-air authority.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: You don't wanna be introduced as... superman. Do you?

jokes.text: Larry asking Darlene about Dean Cain: 'What's Superman's name?' / 'Clark Kent.' / 'No, no, no. The actor.' / 'Christopher Reeve.' / 'The new one.' / 'Dean Cain?'
jokes.setup: Larry wants to contact Dean Cain after learning he's cohosting with him.
jokes.punchline: He doesn't know Dean Cain's name — asks for 'Superman's name' and gets the fictional character, then the original movie actor, before arriving at the actual person.
jokes.explanation: A genuinely well-constructed bit of comic ladder-climbing. Three steps to reach the correct answer, each step funny on its own. 'Clark Kent' from Darlene plays it completely straight. The structure is tight and the execution is clean — this is good sitcom writing.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: That makes no sense.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Of course it does. Sweetheart, it's the network.

jokes.text: Hank calls Dean Cain cold to pitch himself as announcer: 'It's another pleat in your cape.'
jokes.setup: Hank, unable to get the announcer job through proper channels, decides to go directly to his fellow cohost.
jokes.punchline: His opening congratulatory line to Dean Cain — 'It's another pleat in your cape' — is a tortured, bizarre idiom that sort of means 'a feather in your cap' but garbled through Superman imagery.
jokes.explanation: An inspired piece of Hank verbal incompetence. 'Another pleat in your cape' is Hank trying to be clever — merging 'feather in your cap' with Superman's cape — and the result is a mangled idiom that makes zero literal sense but is perfectly logical for Hank. High originality, high character integration (only Hank would invent this phrase), and highly quotable. Earns 8.2.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: One person is a host. 2 or more are cohosts.

jokes.text: Hank's pitch to Dean Cain: 'You don't wanna be introduced as... [pause] ...superman. Do you?' — performing the harelip announcer saying Superman as his evidence.
jokes.setup: Hank is making the case against the existing announcer by demonstrating what it sounds like when a harelip says 'Superman.'
jokes.punchline: The implication that he performs an offensive impression of the speech impediment as a sales technique, then hangs up when he gets no buy-in.
jokes.explanation: Hank's complete lack of self-awareness in his sales pitch — doing an impression of a speech impediment to a stranger to sell himself — is perfectly Hank. The abrupt hang-up when it doesn't work is a good visual button. Slightly undercut by the cringe of the impression itself.

dialogue.line: Rita to bring in the urbanites and the hairdressers

jokes.text: Hank's pitch ends: '...Or Dean Cain. Sure. Whatever you... hello?' — Dean Cain has hung up.
jokes.setup: Hank is mid-pitch, demonstrating flexibility ('Or Dean Cain, sure, whatever you want').
jokes.punchline: Dean Cain hangs up mid-sentence. The joke is the sudden silence where Hank realizes he's been cut off — and his complete obliviousness up to that point.
jokes.explanation: A clean button on the Hank/Dean Cain phone call. The comedy is entirely structural — the hang-up, the pause, Hank saying 'hello?' The moment doesn't need any extra words, and doesn't use them.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: I mean actual hairdressers.

jokes.text: Larry confronts Artie: 'Then what are Rita and Superman, just backups in case I get a paper cut opening one of those envelopes?'
jokes.setup: Larry is furious to discover he's actually a cohost, not the host. Artie insists he's the host, Rita and Dean Cain are the cohosts.
jokes.punchline: Larry's sarcastic reduction of the cohost role to 'backup in case I get a paper cut opening envelopes' — perfectly targeting the envelope-opening ceremony of awards shows.
jokes.explanation: Genuinely witty. The paper cut/envelope gag skewers awards show conventions with precision — it's observational and character-specific simultaneously. Larry's paranoia about status is expressed through an image that's both funny and sharply true about the artificiality of awards shows. Good economy, specific, earned.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, they are a bunch of dickheads, aren't they?

jokes.text: Artie's promise: 'I'm going to make sure that your head is at least 50% larger than theirs on the cover of TV Guide.'
jokes.setup: Larry argues the cohost arrangement is insulting. Artie tries to placate him.
jokes.punchline: Artie's solution to Larry's status anxiety is a literal measurement of head size on a magazine cover — treating TV Guide photo real estate as a legitimate proxy for career standing.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest industry satire moments. The specificity of '50% larger' transforms this from a general joke about celebrity ego into a precise, absurd quantification of it. Artie offering this as a genuine consolation — and it almost working — is character comedy at its best. The fact that TV Guide cover size was genuinely contested in this era deepens it. Earns 8+.

dialogue.line: Well, that doesn't seem that funny, either.

jokes.text: Phil asks to remove the coconut audio and just play 'chicken' over it. Larry: ''Cause it's funny, right? You trust your instincts, kiddo. Always trust Larry's instincts. Always.'
jokes.setup: Phil thinks the chicken line isn't funny either (as the network exec said). Larry reasserts his comedy authority.
jokes.punchline: Larry's grandiose self-validation — 'Always trust Larry's instincts. Always.' — delivered as if it's a piece of timeless wisdom, when the whole episode has shown his instincts producing chaos.
jokes.explanation: Good ironic self-awareness moment — Larry is completely unironic while the show is totally ironic about it. His faith in his own instincts is the central comic delusion of his character, and 'Always trust Larry's instincts. Always.' lands well as an ironic thesis statement for the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Chicken is funny in the context of a smell that goes on your face.

jokes.text: 'One person is a host. Two or more are cohosts.'
jokes.setup: Artie keeps insisting that Larry is 'the host' and the others are 'cohosts.'
jokes.punchline: Larry's flat, definitional rebuttal — stated as if reciting a dictionary — is the most efficient way to expose Artie's sophistry.
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. The joke is a dictionary definition delivered as a devastating put-down. Ten words, total economy, no waste. It's Larry at his most dry and most correct simultaneously, which is rare and therefore funny. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: stevie called me up, and he was crying to me, 'why haven't you given Larry this job? Why don't you ask him to host?' Wee wee wee wee wee.

jokes.text: 'My agent is tearing himself a new asshole.'
jokes.setup: Larry is complaining to Artie about the cohosting situation.
jokes.punchline: The idiom 'tearing himself a new one' expressed in full anatomical detail — delivered without emphasis, just as information.
jokes.explanation: Solid but not exceptional. The joke is just the full-form expression of a common idiom, which Larry Sanders uses as a register of authenticity. Functions well in context but doesn't rise above competent.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: You should call the conan o'brien people, see if they need a producer for the farewell special.

jokes.text: Artie's demographic breakdown of the People's Choice cohost lineup: Superman for 'younguns,' Rita for 'urbanites and the hairdressers,' Larry for 'the rest... just plain folks who like to laugh.'
jokes.setup: Artie explains the network's logic for the three-host arrangement.
jokes.punchline: The demographic breakdown is a masterwork of backhanded complimenting — ending with Larry's constituency being 'just plain folks who like to laugh,' which sounds nice but is clearly the least glamorous category.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best bits of industry satire. The specificity escalates perfectly: Dean Cain/youngsters makes sense; Rita Moreno/urbanites is a stretch; 'hairdressers' is brilliant; and Larry/plain folks is the deflating kicker. The hairdressers qualifier is the standout — it's specific enough to feel like real market research data while being absurd. When Larry asks about 'hairdressers' and Artie confirms 'actual hairdressers,' the meta-joke about research departments over-segmenting is perfect. Earns 8.3.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: No wonder you been married so many times.

jokes.text: 'I mean actual hairdressers. Our research department is giving us incredibly specific stuff these days.'
jokes.setup: Larry asks about the 'hairdressers' demographic with skepticism.
jokes.punchline: Artie doubles down — they mean literal hairdressers, and the research is 'incredibly specific' — playing the absurdity completely straight.
jokes.explanation: The perfect topper to the demographic bit. 'Incredibly specific' delivered as if this is admirable rather than insane is Artie at his deadpan best. The joke simultaneously satirizes network research and Artie's loyalty to institutional absurdity.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Save your Ivy-league double-talk for your chums down at the parliamentary debating society.

jokes.text: Larry accidentally insults the network exec Melanie to her face, then immediately pivots: 'You know, Artie and I were just saying what a nice bunch of network heads we have working here.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are calling the network execs 'a bunch of dickheads' — then Melanie walks up.
jokes.punchline: Larry's instant 180 — 'nice bunch of network heads' — is so clumsy it fools no one, yet everyone plays along.
jokes.explanation: A well-executed cringe beat. The verbal reversal from 'dickheads' to 'nice bunch of network heads' is funny on its own; the fact that Melanie smiles and floats away without acknowledging it makes it more uncomfortable. Classic showbiz social performance. Artie's 'Oh, Melanie! Hi, Melanie!' is a great supporting reaction.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Why is everybody acting like a bunch of 4-year-olds at a fucking barney show?

jokes.text: The network exec Melanie says the chicken line 'doesn't seem that funny, either.' Larry: 'No, chicken is funny in the context of a smell that goes on your face. Trust me.'
jokes.setup: Larry is defending his position that 'chicken' is funnier than 'coconut' as the deodorant smell in the commercial parody.
jokes.punchline: His formal defense — 'chicken is funny in the context of a smell that goes on your face' — is the kind of reductive comedy theory that sounds plausible but is absurd when spoken aloud.
jokes.explanation: Larry articulating comedy theory with total conviction is always funny. 'Trust me' is the perfect, unearned authority kicker. This line is also a meta-joke: the audience has now heard both words in context and can judge for themselves, and the episode's position is that both words are kind of funny, which makes Larry's certainty funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Is that about a specific person or a pet?

jokes.text: Melanie reveals it was Artie's idea to add the cohosts, not the network's — Artie had been blaming the network.
jokes.setup: Artie has been telling Larry the cohost arrangement was the network's demand.
jokes.punchline: Melanie casually exposes Artie's lie: 'That's what Arthur thinks, and we disagree with him. But, as producer, he has final say.'
jokes.explanation: A classic Larry Sanders reversal — the episode's conspiracy is revealed casually by an outsider who has no idea she's dropping a bomb. Melanie's breezy 'have a good one' exit makes it worse. Good misdirection payoff that reframes the entire Artie plot. Strong structure.

dialogue.line: I don't think so.

jokes.text: 'I do that all the time. Don't make a big deal out of it.' — Artie admits he routinely blames decisions on 'the network.'
jokes.setup: Larry confronts Artie about blaming the network for his own cohosting decision.
jokes.punchline: Artie's confession is casual and completely unapologetic — 'I do that all the time' — as if this is a known, unremarkable management technique.
jokes.explanation: A perfect Artie line. The admission that he routinely blame-shifts to 'the network' is delivered as professional wisdom, not a confession. 'Don't make a big deal out of it' is spectacular — Artie isn't even flustered. This is Rip Torn's character at its most essential: old Hollywood, pragmatic, completely without shame. Earns 8.2.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Coconut. 2 'k' sounds followed by a nut.

jokes.text: The reveal that Larry's agent Stevie called Artie to lobby for Larry to host — which Larry denies instigating — while his denial is being laughed off.
jokes.setup: Larry claims he never wanted the People's Choice job. Artie reveals that an hour after their conversation, Stevie called pleading for Larry to be given the hosting gig.
jokes.punchline: Artie's impression of Stevie: 'Why haven't you given Larry this job? Why don't you ask him to host? Wee wee wee wee wee.' — Artie reduces Stevie's advocacy to pig squealing.
jokes.explanation: Artie imitating the agent's whining as 'Wee wee wee wee wee' is a great piece of Rip Torn physical/vocal comedy (inferred). The joke is also structurally satisfying: it exposes Larry's self-deception (he clearly told Stevie to call) while Artie reveals he's been managing this all along. Good character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Mr. Hal linden.

jokes.text: Artie: 'Oh, yeah, you could produce four more shows simultaneously. Fucking A.' / 'You should call the Conan O'Brien people, see if they need a producer for the farewell special.' / 'Good idea. So give me a call, and I'll let you host that one, too.'
jokes.setup: Larry and Artie are in a full argument, trading passive-aggressive jabs about each other's workload and competence.
jokes.punchline: Artie's escalating counter-offer — 'I'll let you host that one, too' — is mock-magnanimous, framing the cohosting insult as a pattern of generosity.
jokes.explanation: A solid escalation exchange. The Conan O'Brien reference is topical (O'Brien had recently taken over The Tonight Show from Leno-adjacent drama). The 'farewell special' jab works as industry shade. Not the sharpest beat in the argument but maintains the momentum.

dialogue.speaker: Elvis Costello
dialogue.line: Don't gimme any more of that big fan shite.

jokes.text: 'No wonder you've been married so many times.'
jokes.setup: The Larry-Artie argument is escalating, with Larry trying to get the last word.
jokes.punchline: Artie's non sequitur personal attack — 'No wonder you've been married so many times' — pivots from professional to personal in a way that's both devastating and completely irrelevant to the argument.
jokes.explanation: A sharp, economical escalation button. The pivot to Larry's personal life as the trump card in a professional argument is classic Artie — he fights dirty when he needs to. Works particularly well because Garry Shandling's multiple marriages were publicly known, giving it an extra real-world sting.

dialogue.speaker: Elvis Costello
dialogue.line: Well, at least he was funny.

jokes.text: Larry storms out: 'You know what? I'm not doing your little People's Choice Awards show, OK? I'm out!'
jokes.setup: The argument between Larry and Artie has fully boiled over.
jokes.punchline: Larry's petulant 'I'm out!' — complete with 'little' to diminish the show — is a childish exit from an adult argument.
jokes.explanation: A functional escalation beat. 'Your little People's Choice Awards show' is good — the possessive makes it childish. The 'I'm out' is a bit generic but serves the narrative. Competent without being exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: This reminds me of the time angela lansbury was on.

jokes.text: Chicken take plays correctly — 'Mmm, tastes a little like chicken.' — after Hank's coconut version was supposed to be out.
jokes.setup: The whole episode's editing war finally resolves: the chicken take is in, the coconut take is out.
jokes.punchline: The take plays. It is... fine. Which is the joke — all this chaos for 'Mmm, tastes a little like chicken.'
jokes.explanation: A meta-joke that works primarily on structure. The 'chicken' take is presented as the correct answer, yet its comedy is minimal — which retroactively validates the network exec who said it wasn't funny. The whole episode has been about this moment, and the moment is exactly as anticlimactic as it deserves to be.

dialogue.speaker: Artie
dialogue.line: Rule number one... never quit. Always make them fire you. That way, you get your money.

jokes.text: Phil to Artie on whether he changed the tape at Larry's request: 'I did not initiate the change, but I was implicated in the course of events that led to the...' / Artie: 'Please, please, please. Save your Ivy-league double-talk for your chums down at the parliamentary debating society.'
jokes.setup: Artie demands a straight answer from Phil about who changed the commercial parody tape.
jokes.punchline: Phil's evasive, legalistic non-answer is met with Artie's magnificently contemptuous 'Ivy-league double-talk... parliamentary debating society' dismissal.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. Phil's passive-voice bureaucratic dodge ('I was implicated in the course of events that led to the...') is pitch-perfect comedy writing for a corporate self-protector. Artie's response is exactly the right length and tone — 'parliamentary debating society' is inspired. The two characters are perfectly counterposed. High character integration for both. Earns 8.2.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I just pulled something. I just... right here.

jokes.text: Artie's line: 'Save your Ivy-league double-talk for your chums down at the parliamentary debating society.'
jokes.setup: Phil is giving a mealy-mouthed non-answer about the tape situation.
jokes.punchline: Artie's cutting dismissal of Phil's language is deployed with absolute authority and precision — the specificity of 'parliamentary debating society' is key.
jokes.explanation: A standout Artie line. The phrase 'parliamentary debating society' is so specifically old-guard establishment that it perfectly captures Artie's disdain for Phil's educated evasiveness. The 'chums' is an affectation that reveals Artie mocking Phil's class background. Only Rip Torn's Artie delivers this. Justifies 8+.

dialogue.speaker: Rita Moreno
dialogue.line: I don't think he dances.

jokes.text: Phil: 'Larry told me to do it.' / Artie: 'And you just automatically do whatever the hell Larry tells you to do?' / Phil: 'Yes, don't you?' / Artie: 'Yes. Now get the hell out of my office.'
jokes.setup: Artie demands accountability for who changed the tape.
jokes.punchline: Phil's 'Yes, don't you?' and Artie's immediate 'Yes. Now get the hell out of my office.' — both men admit to blind Larry-worship, which ends the conversation.
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke structurally. The setup is Phil's frank admission that he did it because Larry said to. Artie's indignant follow-up question ('And you just automatically do whatever Larry tells you to do?') sets up what appears to be a lecture on professional independence. Phil's 'Yes, don't you?' flips the power dynamic entirely. Artie's 'Yes. Now get the hell out of my office.' is the perfect button — it validates Phil's behavior, ends his own moral authority, and gets him out of an uncomfortable conversation simultaneously. Three lines, total economy, maximum character specificity. Near-perfect structure. Earns 8.7.

dialogue.speaker: Hank
dialogue.line: Mmm, tastes a little like coconut.

jokes.text: 'What's in the bag?' — The Elvis Costello autograph LP that was specifically forbidden.
jokes.setup: The entire staff has been warned not to ask Elvis Costello for autographs because he's temperamental.
jokes.punchline: Someone is carrying a concealed Elvis Costello album — caught red-handed — which they reveal sheepishly as 'Spike.'
jokes.explanation: A solid visual-derived setup beat that plants the autograph gag for later payoff. The sheepishness of the reveal ('OK, it's Elvis Costello. Spike.') is appropriately embarrassed. Good economy.

jokes.text: 'Why is everybody acting like a bunch of 4-year-olds at a fucking Barney show?'
jokes.setup: Everyone on staff is obsessing over Elvis Costello's presence, wanting autographs despite being told not to.
jokes.punchline: Larry's comparison of his professional TV staff to children at a Barney concert is both apt and hypocritical (he was just asking about 'Pump It Up').
jokes.explanation: A good line that gains extra resonance as self-aware irony: Larry is the one who wanted Elvis to play his favorite song and got banned from talking to Michael Bolton. 'Barney show' is a sharp, era-specific image. Good character hypocrisy joke.

jokes.text: Larry to Elvis Costello: 'Elvis, I heard you coming down the hall. Hi. I'm a big fan. Listen, you know the song 'Alison'... I was just wondering about this. Is that... is that... excuse me.' — then Artie pulls him away.
jokes.setup: Larry was specifically warned not to bring up 'Pump It Up' or ask personal questions. He approaches Elvis anyway.
jokes.punchline: He immediately launches into a personal question about 'Alison' — is it about a specific person or a pet? — before being interrupted. The Michael Bolton callback is now fully active.
jokes.explanation: The Michael Bolton callback pays off here. Larry does EXACTLY what he was told not to do, and the question ('Is it about a specific person or a pet?') is the most awkward possible version of it. Artie's interruption saves him — barely. Good cringe escalation leading to the Elvis meltdown.

jokes.text: Artie, trying to charm Elvis Costello: 'You know, I've always wanted to ask you about your song 'Alison.' Is that about a specific person or a pet?'
jokes.setup: Artie has just interrupted Larry to stop him from asking uncomfortable questions of Elvis Costello.
jokes.punchline: Artie immediately asks the exact same question Larry was just interrupted for asking.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's structural gems. Artie rescues Larry from asking the question, then asks the exact same question himself — without any self-awareness. The 'Alison... is it about a specific person or a pet?' lands harder the second time because we've just been set up for it. The 'or a pet' addition is pure gold — it's the kind of question that would genuinely offend a musician who has written a devastating song. Near-perfect structure. Earns 8.6.

jokes.text: Hank meets Elvis Costello backstage: 'Hank, this is Elvis.' / 'I don't think so.'
jokes.setup: Paula introduces Hank to Elvis Costello backstage.
jokes.punchline: 'I don't think so.' — Hank's flat denial of Elvis Costello's identity, either because he doesn't know who he is or because he expected the other Elvis.
jokes.explanation: Four words. Maximum economy. 'I don't think so.' is devastating in context — Hank is either (a) genuinely confused because 'Elvis' should be Presley, (b) dismissing Costello as insufficiently Elvis, or (c) just being Hank. All three readings are funny. The line works on every level. High quotability. Earns 8.4.

jokes.text: Hank interrupts Elvis Costello's performance to lobby Artie for the People's Choice announcer job.
jokes.setup: Elvis Costello is performing 'Thirteen Steps Lead Down' on the live show. Hank sidles up to Artie on the studio floor to make his announcer pitch.
jokes.punchline: The contrast between the live musical performance happening feet away and Hank's whispering career lobbying is the joke — the audacity of using this moment for personal advancement.
jokes.explanation: The audacity is the joke. Hank lobbying for a job during a live musical performance captures everything wrong with him as a professional and as a human — oblivious to the moment, focused entirely on his own advancement. Good cringe comedy.

jokes.text: Hank to Artie during the Elvis performance: 'I've spoken to Rita Moreno and Superman. And they don't seem to want to help. Fuckers.'
jokes.setup: Hank reports back on his canvassing of fellow People's Choice cohosts for support on the announcer gig.
jokes.punchline: 'Fuckers.' — said in a low, resigned voice mid-performance, directed at Rita Moreno and Superman.
jokes.explanation: The deadpan 'Fuckers.' aimed at Superman and Rita Moreno for not supporting Hank's announcer gig is absurd and perfectly delivered. The word does all the work — no elaboration needed. The context (whispered during a live performance) amplifies it.

jokes.text: Hank: 'Coconut is funnier than chicken. Coconut. Two 'k' sounds followed by a nut.'
jokes.setup: Hank is told Larry has quit the People's Choice so he can't help with the announcer gig.
jokes.punchline: Hank shifts immediately to the other grievance — the coconut line — and delivers a formal comedy theory defense: 'Two k sounds followed by a nut.'
jokes.explanation: The episode's comic crown jewel. Hank's formal comedy theory — 'Two k sounds followed by a nut' — is simultaneously (a) correct (k-sounds and 'nut' are genuinely funny phonetically, this is real comedy theory), (b) a devastating vindication of his position over Larry's, and (c) delivered in the most Hank-possible way: as a whispered aside during Elvis Costello's live performance. The specificity of the analysis, the timing, and the callback to the entire episode's running argument make this the highest-impact joke in the episode. Earns 8.8.

jokes.text: Artie offers Larry a replacement host for the People's Choice: 'Mr. Hal Linden.' Larry: 'Hal Linden is good. Hal Linden is funny.' / 'And he'll do one of those dance numbers.'
jokes.setup: Larry has quit the People's Choice and Artie needs a replacement. He offers Hal Linden (Barney Miller star).
jokes.punchline: Larry immediately agrees that Hal Linden is good and funny — revealing that his objections were never about the show's quality but about his own status. 'And he'll do one of those dance numbers' closes the loop on what Larry refused.
jokes.explanation: Larry immediately validating Hal Linden — a TV stalwart of lesser celebrity — as a perfectly good host exposes his own insecurity. If Hal Linden is funny, the show isn't the problem. The dance number callback is a tidy bow on that subplot.

jokes.text: 'OK. I'll just hang there with Hal and twist slowly in the wind.'
jokes.setup: Artie points out that if Larry doesn't take the People's Choice, he's left with whatever the network gives him.
jokes.punchline: Larry's vision of cohosting with Hal Linden as being tied to a pole and left to slowly twist is melodramatic and self-pitying in a very Larry way.
jokes.explanation: A good deadpan self-pity line. 'Twist slowly in the wind' is a slightly elevated idiom that suits Larry's self-dramatizing nature. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Elvis Costello's meltdown: 'And while I'm up there doing my number, you're yap, yap, yap. We were listening most intently. We're huge fans!' — followed by Elvis: 'Don't give me any more of that big fan shite.'
jokes.setup: Elvis Costello is furious that the staff was talking during his performance.
jokes.punchline: Artie's desperate 'We were listening most intently. We're huge fans!' is met with Elvis's contemptuous 'Don't give me any more of that big fan shite.'
jokes.explanation: The cringe payoff of the entire Elvis subplot. 'We were listening most intently' is gloriously arch as a desperate lie; 'big fan shite' is Elvis correctly identifying the hollow currency of late-night celebrity culture. Good escalation structure, high cringe value.

jokes.text: Elvis: 'Letterman, Letterman... that's big fans.' / Larry: 'I thought he didn't do Letterman.' / 'I thought we were the first to have him on.' / 'When did you do Letterman? What was Letterman like?'
jokes.setup: Elvis is complaining that the Larry Sanders Show staff didn't treat him with proper fan reverence.
jokes.punchline: Elvis praises Letterman. Larry and Artie's response is immediate competitive panic — 'I thought we were the first to have him on' — and then pure star-struck fawning: 'What was Letterman like?'
jokes.explanation: A layered bit of industry satire. The Letterman jealousy is real and specific (Letterman was genuinely considered more credible than competitors). 'What was Letterman like?' is the kicker — Larry, in the middle of a crisis, can't help being curious about his rival. The self-sabotage is perfectly in character. Good cringe escalation. Earns 8.

jokes.text: Elvis: 'I've taken care of it meself. Bye-bye.' — He has gotten himself an autograph from Larry without asking.
jokes.setup: Larry offers to do whatever it takes to make it up to Elvis after his meltdown.
jokes.punchline: 'I've taken care of it meself.' — Elvis has already solved the autograph problem by getting Larry's autograph (revealed by 'By the way, Larry, I'm a big fan.').
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed reversal. The autograph ban was to protect Elvis from fan harassment; Elvis turns out to be the fan seeking an autograph. 'By the way, Larry, I'm a big fan.' after the entire meltdown is the perfect button — it recontextualizes the whole scene and exposes Elvis as exactly the kind of person he was complaining about. Sharp misdirection with a clean structural payoff.

jokes.text: Costello says he's 'taken care of it meself' and leaves. Then: 'By the way, Larry, I'm a big fan.' [Costello exits]
jokes.setup: Costello has spent the scene furious at the entire staff for their treatment of him.
jokes.punchline: His parting 'I'm a big fan' — delivered after this entire tirade — is perfectly sardonic. It mirrors the language used to butter him up and weaponizes it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best closing beats. Costello's ironic 'big fan' lands perfectly as a callback to all the 'we're huge fans' language deployed in the episode, now turned back on Larry with surgical contempt. The economy is exceptional — three words do more than the entire preceding scene. Justifies 8.4.

jokes.text: 'What the... look at this. This reminds me of the time Angela Lansbury was on.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is watching the aftermath of Elvis's meltdown in stunned silence.
jokes.punchline: Artie's unflappable response is to compare it to Angela Lansbury — an iconic, elderly actress known for gentle murder mysteries — as if celebrity meltdowns are routine benchmarks in his career.
jokes.explanation: The Angela Lansbury comparison is inspired — Angela Lansbury and Elvis Costello are the furthest possible points on the celebrity compass. Artie treating a rock star meltdown as comparable to an Angela Lansbury incident reveals his veteran's total equanimity. Perfect Artie character beat. Good economy, high character integration.

jokes.text: 'This reminds me of the time Angela Lansbury was on.' [implication that something similarly disastrous happened]
jokes.setup: The Costello disaster has just concluded.
jokes.punchline: Artie's institutional memory produces Angela Lansbury as the comparison — an absurd contrast of personalities — implying that sweet Murder She Wrote also resulted in a backstage blowup.
jokes.explanation: A great Artie implication joke. We never hear what happened with Lansbury, but the juxtaposition with Costello's meltdown suggests she was equally disastrous backstage. The image of Angela Lansbury causing a scene is inherently funny. Only Artie has this institutional context.

jokes.text: Artie reveals he quit the People's Choice (or got fired): 'So I told 'em... just take your tap shoes and shove 'em up your collective ass.' / Larry: 'You quit?' / Artie: 'No. They fired me.'
jokes.setup: Artie says he came to tell Larry he was wrong to involve him in the cohosting situation and quit.
jokes.punchline: 'You quit?' / 'No. They fired me. Rule number one — never quit. Always make them fire you. That way, you get your money.'
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in Artie wisdom. 'Never quit. Always make them fire you. That way, you get your money.' is old Hollywood pragmatism delivered as timeless philosophy. The reveal that 'quitting' and 'being fired' are the same event — just framed differently — is both funny and genuinely wise. High quotability, perfect character integration. Earns 8.4.

jokes.text: Artie reveals how he quit the People's Choice: 'I told 'em — just take your tap shoes and shove 'em up your collective ass.' / 'You quit?' / 'No. They fired me. Rule number one — never quit. Always make them fire you. That way, you get your money.'
jokes.setup: Artie dramatically describes telling the People's Choice to 'shove their tap shoes.'
jokes.punchline: He immediately clarifies this was not quitting — they fired him. And the reason for the distinction is purely financial ('you get your money'). The principle is revealed as ruthless pragmatism dressed as principle.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's finest jokes and a perfect Artie speech. The setup (dramatic resignation speech) is immediately deflated (they fired me, actually). The rule — 'never quit, always make them fire you' — is delivered as timeless industry wisdom and IS timeless industry wisdom. The structure is near-perfect: setup, reversal, explanation. The character integration is total — only Artie Ripp Torn) has both the gravitas to deliver the rule and the shamelessness to follow it. Comparable to the calibration anchors in quality. Justifies 8.75.

jokes.text: Larry: 'I felt so bad about our little argument last night that I woke up and... I signed the contract to cohost the People's Choice Awards as a favor to you.' / Artie: 'Oh, shit.'
jokes.setup: Both men arrive to apologize to each other. Each expects the other to have fixed the problem.
jokes.punchline: Larry has signed the contract — locking them both in — at the exact moment Artie has quit/been fired. They are now in the worst possible position: Larry is cohosting without a producer.
jokes.explanation: A superb ironic reversal. Both men's gestures of reconciliation — Artie quitting, Larry signing — have created a new crisis that's worse than the original. 'Oh, shit.' from Artie is the perfect reaction: the man who never loses his cool, genuinely caught. The structure is excellent — classic sitcom double-reversal with real character stakes. Earns 8.4.

jokes.text: Larry at the People's Choice rehearsal, trying to introduce Rita Moreno, getting corrected on blocking, then attempting the step-kick dance number and immediately pulling something.
jokes.setup: Larry, who specifically refused to do dance numbers, is now at the People's Choice rehearsal being taught to do exactly that.
jokes.punchline: 'Kick, step, step, step. Kick, step, step, step. Now catch my leg. Catch my... there you go. I just pulled something. I just... right here.' — Larry immediately injures himself on the first dance attempt.
jokes.explanation: The physical payoff of Larry's earlier refusal to do dance numbers. He's now doing exactly what he said he wouldn't, and his body immediately betrays him. 'I just pulled something. I just... right here.' is a perfect character beat — delivered with his usual neurotic precision about his own physical state. Good slapstick escalation.

jokes.text: 'I don't think he dances.'
jokes.setup: Larry has just pulled a muscle attempting the step-kick routine and retreated to the side.
jokes.punchline: An observer delivers the most understated possible post-mortem: 'I don't think he dances.'
jokes.explanation: Six words, perfect economy. The observer's matter-of-fact assessment after watching a man pull a muscle on the first step-kick is the ideal deadpan button. It doesn't editorialize beyond the obvious. One of the best reaction beats in the episode.

jokes.text: Rita Moreno tries to encourage Larry to commit to the dance: 'I know this is unfamiliar territory. You feel a little out of place here.' / Larry: 'Just a tad.'
jokes.setup: Rita is trying to coach Larry through his obvious discomfort at the People's Choice rehearsal.
jokes.punchline: 'Just a tad.' — Larry's understatement of the century.
jokes.explanation: A clean deadpan understatement. 'Just a tad' is Larry accepting the premise with maximum economy. Not a standout joke but a solid character beat.

jokes.text: The People's Choice opening announcement: '35 years of daytime dramas' — then Hank's coconut line plays.
jokes.setup: Larry is at the People's Choice rehearsal, finally in the place he was maneuvered into. The opening announcement plays.
jokes.punchline: 'Mmm, tastes a little like coconut.' — Hank's line has now migrated from the Larry Sanders commercial parody to the People's Choice Awards opening. The coconut line has conquered everything.
jokes.explanation: The perfect episode-closing joke. The coconut line — which has been fought over, mocked, analyzed, broadcast against everyone's wishes — ends the episode by appearing one final time in a completely new context: the People's Choice Awards itself. It's a structural masterstroke. The coconut line outlasted everyone who tried to suppress it, it migrated from one show to another, and it gets the last word. The joke is funnier here than any of its previous appearances because of everything it represents. Near-perfect structure, economy, and callback integration. Deserves the highest score in the episode.

tmdb_overview: Artie is chosen to produce the People's Choice Awards, prompting both Larry and Hank to try for a role in the show.
